notes.text: Almost every Telugu word ends in a vowel. That is why old poets called it the Italian of the East.
Namaskaram fits any hour, but with friends people just ask emiti sangathi: so, what is the matter?
Telugu shows respect in the verb ending, not the pronoun. Meeru vasthara sounds warmer than nuvvu vastava.
Your father's sister is atta, your mother's brother is mama, and their child is the one you may marry.
Gongura, the sour red leaf, has no English name. Andhra kitchens turn it into a pickle people ship worldwide.
Counting money, people still say oka veyyi for a thousand but jump to laksha, not hundred thousand.
Pachcha means green, but pachchi means raw or unripe. Same root: what is fresh is what is green.
Ask for the road as daari or roddu. Both work, and roddu is simply English road wearing Telugu clothes.
Repu means tomorrow and mundu means before, yet mundu also means ahead. Time and space share one word.
Shopkeepers say enta and you answer with a lower number. Bargaining is expected in markets, never in shops.
To say you are ill, Telugu says the illness came to you: naaku jwaram vachchindi, fever came to me.
Illu is a house, but pandiri is the leafy canopy tied outside for weddings. Every home needs one once.
Pani covers job, chore, and errand alike. Pani undi can mean anything from a meeting to washing rice.
Feelings sit in the manasu, the mind heart. Manasu baaledu means sad, literally my mind is not well.
Ugadi new year starts with pachchadi, six tastes in one bite, teaching that a year holds all of them.
